item.title: ADCN: NCAA Labor Market, Data Quality, News
item.dc:creator: Brad Stenger
item.description:
NCAA Labor Market is a Mess but may not be Total Chaos

The Ninth Circuit federal appeals court upheld the NCAA’s 5-in-5 eligibility rule where student-athletes get five consecutive years of college sports athletic eligibility. Sort of.

The 3-judge panel stayed consistent with precedent, acknowledging that the restrains competition with its unilateral decisions on labor criteria and enforcement. The NCAA is is a monopsony (the opposite of a monopoly), the singular buyer in a market (as opposed to seller). Still, the NCAA, and not the defendent, won this appeal judgement.

The appeals court decided that while the defendent had been excluded from continuing a college baseball career due to the end of his NCAA-determined eligibility, his exclusion was not anti-competitive in terms of the college baseball labor market. The judge who authored the opinion, Gabriel Sanchez, wrote (via Courthouse News Service) that labor markets differ from sport to sports so, in legal terms, “Markets are not interchangeable.”

The situation reveals how difficult it will be determine college athlete employee rights. If each intercollegiate sport is its own labor market, then each sport will probably need its own collective bargaining agreement or, if decision forum is courts, lots of case-by-case legislation.

The American Bar Association lays out how (paywall), in another recent 10th Circuit court ruling, college athletes who graduated last spring should, in fact, be fifth-year eligible, “From a monopsony perspective, the district court suggested, the fact that some workers may benefit from restricted competition does not justify buyer-side coordination that harms the labor market overall.”

The labor market for college football has become a lot more stable after a few turbulent weeks leading up to the season. Conferences have opportunities to set and enforce rules that affect who can and cannot play, and because those rules only apply to part of the labor market, they are not anti-competitive. A good rundown comes from Michael McCann at Sportico.

LSU might want dubious athletes to play for the school but, unless they want to leave the Southeastern Conference, they will not risk violations of the conference’s member-agreed rules. And conferences are now quite willing to use court actions to enforce those rules.

The universities, the athletic conferences, and the NCAA all have business models. The decision-making for universities and for conferences that differentiate one from the next is apparent. Student populations, alumni resources, media markets, long-held traditions, organizational structures, institutional priorities are factors.

The NCAA does not seem to have quite so many different levers to pull. It will be far easier to operate if federal legislation provides it with an anti-trust excemption that will keep its monopsony intact.

Athletes have the right to choose a school, something that comes down to compensation, NIL opportunities, and relationships with coaches and teammates. What passes for student-athlete employments is still to be determined.

Both the NCAA and college athletes face complications and, possibly, hardship, if each sport (and with it, each gender) has to figure out its path forward.

Randy Levine, part of President Trump’s Saving College Sports roundtable, spoke with Sportico’s McCann after federal legislation failed. Levine said that without laws in place, “The disparity between big and small schools will multiply in record speed, and student athletes will continue to lose scholarships, health protections and not get paid for their services.”

In reality, the chaos is exaggerated. With each court judgement the challenge that college sports faces clears up. Not that it makes any of it easier, the legal judgements actually show the enormous amount of work it will take to put viable, sustainable, fair employment rights for student-athletes in place.

Data Supply and Quality Issues

The Carnegie Mellon Sports Analytics Conference will again feature a reproducible research contest. Get your submissions in. Reproducibility is important, but it has its challenges.

A new report from World Bank shows that reproducibility failures has inhibited policy advances that could, in theory, improve populations’ health and well-being.

The Institute for Replication checked data repositories that were set up for research studies’ reproductions. The organization found 21 percent of the repositories contained personal identifiable information.

The UK Biobank is gigantic human health information resource (500,000+ participants). The data is de-identified and access to the data is controlled. But there have been large-scale leaks, and re-identification of the data is possible.

Openness, privacy. and security are not the only supply-side quality measures for data. The European Conference on Computer Vision will hold a workshop on curated data. Smaller, higher quality data sets can improve machine learning objectives.

Synthetic data is also finding a role in many analysis pipelines. Industry consultant, Kathy Lange, says that it is best used as a supplementary tool for real-world data, and not as a replacement.

An example, synthetic data improves image-recognition models when real-world data is limited. Synthetic images improved a North Carolina State research model’s ability to recognize trees when real images were limited, But synthetic data miss subtle details and lack nature’s variation.

Data sharing increases the importance of data quality measures like these. Sports does not share data as much as it could, and that might be, in part, because the benefit has not been spelled out, while the inconvenience of sharing is more obvious.
